How many souls have been made offerings to the gods, and how many female infants buried alive, and how many wives thrown into the fire along with their dead husbands. Is there, after the likes of this, any further baseness in morals and feebleness of judgment?

Attributing the returning to God the Exalted is a figurative attribution, because He brings into being the high causes and the system of their interaction and opposition within the subsidiary causes, until they reach the immediate causes, in the manner of attributing the extending and withdrawal of the shade to Him, the Exalted, in His saying: "Have you not seen how your Lord extended the shadow?" [al-Furqan: 45] up to His saying: "Then We withdrew it to Us, a gradual withdrawal" [al-Furqan: 46], and in the manner of the attribution in the saying of people: "The emir built the city of such-and-such."

It is also permissible that "asfala safilin" be a locative (adverbial of place), that is: a place lower than what the lowest dwell in; so the annexing of "asfala" to "safilin" is the annexing of the place to what dwells in it. "Asfala" is in the accusative by "radadnahu" in the manner of an adverbial of place, or by removal of the preposition, that is: to the lowest of the low; and that is the abode of punishment, like His saying: "Indeed the hypocrites are in the lowest level of the Fire" [al-Nisa: 145]. So "radd" is used metaphorically for the meaning of placing him in a place that he deserves, and the attribution of "radd" to God the Exalted on this aspect is literal.

I reckon that His saying the Exalted, "Then We returned him to the lowest of the low," was the basis from which Malik, may God have mercy on him, derived what 'Iyad mentioned in al-Madarik. He said: Ibn Abi Uways said: Malik said: Rabi'ah approached me one day and said to me: "Who is the 'safilah' (base person), O Malik?" I said: "One who eats with his religion." He said to me: "Then who is the basest of the base?" I said: "One who makes others eat with his religion." So he said: "Zih" [an exclamation of approval], and he struck my chest (i.e., he struck my chest, meaning in approval). And that the polytheists were the lowest of the low because their great men and their leaders shaded them, so they made the worship of idols seem attractive to them, in order that they might attain their leadership.

[Page 421]

*Wal-tini waz-zaytun* (By the fig and the olive).
*Wa-tur sinin* (And by Mount Sinai).
*Wa-hadha al-baladi al-amin* (And by this secure city).
*Laqad khalaqna al-insana fi ahsani taqwim* (We have certainly created man in the best of stature).
*Thumma radadnahu asfala safilin* (Then We returned him to the lowest of the low).

The opening of the speech with a emphatic oath indicates the importance of the purpose the speech is directed toward, and the lengthening of the oath is an arousal of interest in what is sworn to.

As for *al-tin* (the fig), its apparent meaning is the well-known fruit bearing this name. It is a fruit whose shape resembles that of the pear, with a skin whose color is bluish-black. Its varieties differ in the darkness of their skin. It is easy to peel and contains something like a white container in its middle, filled with honey of pleasant fragrance mixed with tiny seeds like small sesame. It is among the best fruits in appearance, taste, and ease of chewing. Its condition indicates the precision of God's craftsmanship and points to His knowledge and power. So swearing by it is for the sake of its indication of divine attributes, just as one swears by the Name for its indication of the Essence, together with a reminder of God's favor upon people, since He created for them this fruit that grows in all lands and that is easy to cultivate, requiring no great labor or treatment.

*Al-zaytun* (the olive) also, its apparent meaning is the well-known fruit that has the oil pressed from it, which people eat and use for light. Swearing by it is like swearing by the fig in that it indicates the attributes of God, together with an allusion to the blessing of creating this beneficial, wholesome fruit that suffices people for their food needs and for their lighting.

Upon the apparent meaning of the two names, *al-tin* and *al-zaytun*, a group of the early exegetes understood them, namely Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, al-Nakha'i, 'Ata', Jabir ibn Zayd, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi, because of the benefits these two fruits have for people, which call for gratitude to Him for having created them for them.

[Page 421 continues]

However, the relevance of mentioning these two alongside "Mount Sinai" and "this secure city" requires that they have a meaning more suitable to the context. It was therefore narrated from Ibn 'Abbas also that *al-tin* is interpreted as the mosque of Noah, which was built on al-Judi after the Flood. Perhaps the naming of this mountain *al-tin* is due to the abundance of figs on it, for a land may be named after what abounds in it of trees, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*Amarkh diyaruhum am 'ushar*

And it was named *al-tin* a place that came in the poetry of al-Nabigha describing clouds in his saying:

*Suhb al-zilal atayna al-tin 'an 'urud * * * yuzjina ghaythan qalilan ma'uhu shabima*

And *al-zaytun* is applied to the mountain on which the Aqsa Mosque was built, because it produces olives. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, Qatada, 'Ikrima, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

In my opinion, it is also permissible that the oath by *al-tin wal-zaytun* means by them the trees of these two fruits, that is, that the two kinds have acquired nobility among trees by the fact that much of them grows in these two sacred places, as Jarir said:

*Ataddhuru hina tasqulu 'aridayha * * * bi-farʻi bashamatin suqiya al-bashamu*

So he invoked water upon the kind of *basham* (a fragrant shrub) for the sake of the branch of the beloved Bashama.

As for *Tur Sinin*, it is the mountain known as "Mount Sinai." *Tur* means "mountain" in the language of the Nabataeans, who are the Canaanites. This mountain became known as *Tur Sinin* because it lies in the desert of *Sinin*, and *Sinin* is a dialectal form of *Sin*, which is the desert between Egypt and the lands of Palestine. It was said: *Sinin* is the name of trees in Nabataean or in Abyssinian, and it was said: its meaning is "beauty" in the language of Abyssinia.

Its arabization has come in a form resembling the form of the sound masculine plural, though it is not a plural. It is therefore permissible in its *i'rab* (grammatical inflection) to inflect it like the inflection of the masculine plural with *waw* in place of *damma*, or *ya'* in place of *fatha* or *kasra*, and it may be left indeclinable on the *ya'* while its *nun* takes the vowels of inflection, like *Siffin* and *Yabrin*. This was previously mentioned at the saying of God, Exalted: ﴿By the Mount [al-Tur]﴾ [al-Tur: 1] ﴿and a Book inscribed﴾ [al-Tur: 2].

[Page 422]

*Al-baladu al-amin* is Mecca. It was called "the secure" because whoever enters it is safe. So *al-amin* is *fa'il* in the sense of *muf'il* (active sense: "making secure"), like *al-da'i al-sami'* in the verse of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib. It is also permissible that it be in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive sense: "made secure") by way of metaphorical attribution, meaning: the one whose inhabitants are secured. God, Exalted, said: ﴿and He gave them security from fear﴾ [Quraysh: 4].

The pointing to it is for glorification, and because the revelation of the surah was in that city, it is present before the eyes and ears of the addressees, like His saying: ﴿I swear by this city﴾ [al-Balad: 1].

According to what has been mentioned of the two latter interpretations of *al-tin* and *al-zaytun*, the relevance between the oaths is complete, and they become an indication of the sources of the greatest of the divine laws revealed to humankind. Thus *al-tin* is an allusion to the message of Noah, which was the first law given to a messenger. *Al-zaytun* is an allusion to the law of Abraham, for he built the Aqsa Mosque as was reported in the hadith, and this was mentioned earlier at the beginning of the Night Journey. *Tur Sinin* is an allusion to the law of the Torah, and *al-baladu al-amin* is an allusion to the place of descent of the law of Islam. There is no allusion to the law of Jesus, because it is a completion of the law of the Torah.

It may be that *al-zaytun*, when interpreted as a place, and as the Aqsa Mosque, is an allusion to the place where the law of Jesus, peace be upon him, appeared, because the Aqsa Mosque was built by Solomon, peace be upon him, and no law descended in it before the law of Jesus. And the saying ﴿and this secure city﴾ would be an allusion to the law of Abraham and the law of Islam, for Islam came upon the foundations of the *hanifiyya* (the primordial monotheistic faith). By this, the allusion of this verse becomes what was stated explicitly in His saying, Exalted: ﴿He has ordained for you of religion that which He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We revealed to you, and that which We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus﴾ [al-Shura: 13]. Thus the order of the allusions to the laws of Noah, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon them all, is not in the order of their appearance. The explanation for the departure of the mentioned order from the external order is that it observes the pairing of the two names derived from the names of the two fruits, and the comparison of the two names indicating two kinds of places on earth, so that the rhetorical device of *muraʻat al-nazir* (the matching of counterparts) and the device of *tawriya* (double meaning) may be achieved, and so that *Sinin* may suit the rhyme endings of the surah.

In the beginning of the surah, the oath by what includes the intention of the descent places of the most famous divine religions is a masterful *istihlal* (opening) for the purpose of the surah, which is that God created man in the best of stature, that is, He created him upon the sound *fitra* (natural disposition), perceiving the proofs of the existence of the Creator and His oneness. In it is an allusion that whatever contradicts that among sects and creeds has deviated from the foundations of all the divine laws, regardless of their differences in the branches, and the meaning of the mastery of the opening is sufficiently established by the possibility that appears in the meaning.

[Page 423]

The clause ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾, together with what is conjoined to it, is the answer to the oath.

The oath upon it indicates that the stature is a hidden stature and that the return is a hidden return, which requires contemplation to perceive, as we will clarify in His saying: ﴿in the best of stature﴾. Therefore it was appropriate that it be confirmed by the emphasis of the oath, because the conduct of most people in their beliefs proceeds in a state resembling that of those who deny that they were created upon the *fitra*.

*Al-khalq* (creation) is the bringing into existence and origination of a thing. God's creating all people means that He created the foundations of existence and originated the first principles at the beginning of creation, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿for that which I created with My two hands﴾ [Sad: 75]. And He created the causes by which the branches are generated from the roots, so their offspring multiplied from them, as He said: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you, then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam﴾ [al-A'raf: 11].

The definiteness of *al-insan* may be the definiteness of the genus, which is the definiteness in which the quiddity is considered together with its existence in the external world, within some or all of its individuals.

It is interpreted to mean: We created all people in the best of stature.

It is also possible that the definiteness of *al-insan* is the definiteness of reality, like the saying: "The man is better than the woman," and the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*al-harbu awwala ma takunu fatiyyatun*

In this case the individuals of the genus are not considered, rather what is considered is the state of the quiddity in its origin, apart from what befalls its individuals that alters some of its characteristics. Among this is the definiteness in His saying, Exalted: ﴿Indeed man was created anxious﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 19], which was discussed earlier in the surah of al-Ma'arij.

*Al-taqwim* is making a thing stand in *qiwam* (with the qaf pronounced with a fatha), meaning: justice and proportion. The best of *taqwim* is its most complete and most fitting for the species of humankind, that is, the best stature for it. This requires that it be a stature specific to humans, which no other creature shares with them. This becomes clear in the proportioning of the outward and inward faculties, such that none of his faculties causes him to fall into what corrupts him, nor does one of his faculties hinder another from performing its function. For others of his kind were below him in this stature.

The particle *fi* (in) indicates the metaphorical sense of containment, borrowed to mean possession and ownership. It is therefore used in the sense of the preposition *bi* of accompaniment or the preposition *li* of possession. The turn away from one of the two literal particles for this meaning to the particle of containment was made to convey the strength of the accompaniment or the strength of possession together with brevity. Were it not for brevity, the equivalent wording would have been: "We have certainly created man with a firm stature which is the best stature."

The verse thus conveys that God formed man with an innate formation proportionate to what He created his species for, in terms of the preparations for its order and civilization. The outward physical form of man is not what is considered by God, Exalted, nor is it worthy of being sworn upon, since it has no effect on the reform of the self, the reform of others, or reform on earth. And if it were what was intended, the relevance found in the oath by the fig, the olive, Tur Sinin, and the secure city would be lost. Rather, what is intended is what completes the proportioning of the self. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed God does not look at your bodies, nor at your forms, but He looks at your hearts." For the intellect is the most noble of what the species of man has been singled out with among all species.

So what is pleasing to God is the proportioning of man's perception and his correct rational outlook, because that is what the actions of the body issue from, since the body is an instrument serving the intellect. Therefore this is what is meant by His saying, Exalted: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾.

As for the creation of the human body in the best of stature, it has no connection to the purpose of the surah. This becomes most clear in His saying: ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾, for if the "return to the lowest of the low" were interpreted as the man's arrival, in the most abject age, at the deficiencies of his strength, as many exegetes explained it, then its remoteness from the purpose of the surah would be even greater, and this is not something in which the listeners' doubt arises such that it would require emphasis by an oath. This is supported by His saying after it: ﴿except those who believe﴾, because faith is the effect of the proportioning of the human intellect, which inspires him to walk in his deeds upon the most upright path, and to treat members of his species who are free from his enmity as one treats the good, in accordance with their agreement with him in the truth. This is the basic principle in the formation of man, when he is safe from the preventing accidents that may befall him from some of that while still in the womb, either by a defect that afflicts him due to an illness of one of his parents, or by the corruption of his frame from a fall or a blow during pregnancy. And what befalls him after birth of an intractable disease that leaves an imbalance of his temperament, thereby distorting some of his natural disposition, such as the foolishness of the melancholic and the sugary ones, or the corruption of the deranged, and what he brings upon himself of bad habits, such as drinking intoxicants and taking narcotics, which over a long period leave his reasoning impaired or his resolve weakened.

The Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 95, verses 1–5 (part 2 of 2):

What we take from this verse is that man is created upon the state of the human natural disposition (fitrah), which God originated in the species so that it would be characterized by its effects. This is the complete human fitrah in its perception, a upright perception of what is conveyed by true sensible things, that is, what agrees with the realities of things that are established in the reality of the matter, owing to the soundness of what the sound senses convey, and what the sound intellect receives from that and disposes of through orderly analysis and synthesis. Such that, if misguided indoctrinations, base habits, deviant natures, and harmful thinking kept away from it, or if they gained some power over it, yet it was able to repel them from itself by the proofs of truth and rightness, it would proceed in all its affairs upon uprightness, and nothing would proceed from it except righteous deeds. But it may stumble in the trailing skirts of its delusion and loosen the reins to its desire and lust, so that they cast it into misguidance; or the callers to error may overpower it by the means of intimidation or enticement, so that it follows them willingly or unwillingly. Then it does not linger long before what it has taken on becomes firmly established in it, so it becomes accustomed to it and forgets rightness and right guidance.

This meaning is explained by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "No child is born except upon the fitrah, then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian," and the hadith continues. That is because his parents are the first to undertake his discipline and education, and they are the people most constantly with him in his childhood. They are the ones who instill in his soul the first ideas. So if he is spared the misguidance of his parents, he has already traveled a stretch by his fitrah. Then after that he is subject to numerous influences upon him: if good, then good; if evil, then evil.

The Prophet ﷺ limited it to the two parents because they are the strongest causes of drawing him into their misguidance, and the most insistent upon their child.

The exegetes, past and present, did not turn to explaining "taqwim" (stature/form) in this great sense; rather they restricted "taqwim" to beauty of form. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Kalbi, Ibrahim, and Abu al-'Aliyah. Or to uprightness of stature; it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Or to youth and vigor; it is narrated from 'Ikrimah and Ibn 'Abbas.

What suits the aim of the surah is only that it be interpreted as a mention of a blessing upon man which man reversed by reversing its thanks, so he disbelieved in the Benefactor, and so he was returned to the lowest of the low. Apart from what Ibn 'Atiyyah related from al-Tha'labi, from Abu Bakr ibn Tahir, that he said: "The taqwim of man is his intellect and his perception, which he has been adorned with through discernment." His wording in al-Qurtubi is close to this, with the addition: "he takes his food with his hand." And what al-Fakhr related from al-Asamm, that "in the best stature" is the most perfect intellect, understanding, manners, knowledge, and eloquence.

The verse indicates that man is naturally disposed to good, and that in his constitution is the drawing of benefit and righteousness for himself, and the aversion to what he thinks is falsehood or ruin, and the love of goodness and good deeds. For this reason you see him rejoice in justice and fairness, advise with what he sees as bringing good to others, relieve the distressed, treat people with kindness, become jealous on behalf of the oppressed, and recoil from injustice so long as it is free of an aim to bring him some benefit, or to satisfy a desire he wants to fulfill, or to quench a rage surging in his breast. These passing states come between him and his fitrah for a time, and he inclines toward the speech of preachers, the wise, and the righteous, honors and esteems them, and wishes that they would remain long.

But when an evil lust assails him, adorning for him the commission of corruptions, and he is unable to repel it from himself, he turns to evil deeds, and the advice of advisers and the admonition of preachers become heavy upon him, in degrees, in his aversion to that, according to the measure of desire's domination over his intellect.

For this reason, the default regarding people, according to the majority of jurists and hadith scholars, is goodness, justice, rightness, and good intention.

The clause "then We returned him to the lowest of the low" is coordinated with the clause "We created man in the best stature," so it falls within the scope of the oath.

The pronoun of the absent in His saying "We returned him" refers to man, so the two aspects of definition mentioned earlier apply to it.

"Thumma" (then) indicates a graded (rank-based) delay, as is its manner in coordinating clauses; because returning him to the lowest of the low after his creation enclosed in the best stature is marvelous, since it involves the reversal of what he was constituted upon, and changing an existing state is more wondrous than bringing into being a state that did not exist; and because this clause is the intended purpose of the speech, to establish that those who deviated from the fitrah became the lowest of the low.

The meaning: "Indeed We made him the lowest of the low," or "We placed him in the lowest of the low."

Returning (radd) in its literal sense is restoring what was taken from a person or moved from a place to what was with him. The term "radd" is applied figuratively to making a thing take a state other than the one it had, as a figurative usage through the relation of the general over the specific, as here.

"Asfala" is a superlative: that is, "more base in lowliness," and it is annexed to "safilin" (sāfilīn), that is, those characterized by lowliness. So the intended meaning is "the lowest of the low" in belief in their Creator, by the indication of His saying: "except those who believed."

The literal meaning of "safalah" is lowness of place, and it is commonly applied figuratively to baseness and meanness of soul. So "al-asfal" is the one who is more base than others of his kind.

"Al-safilun" are those of base belief, and polytheism is the lowest of belief, so "asfala safilin" is the second object of "radadnahu," because it is treated in the manner of the sisters of "sara" (to become).

The meaning: man began to change what he was created upon of the stature, which is belief in one God and what that requires of His fear and His vigilance, so he became the lowest of the low. And is there anything lower than one who believes in the divinity of stones and of dumb animals, such as cows, crocodiles, or serpents, or of the acacia tree,
or one who reckons time a god and calls it fate, or one who denies the existence of the Creator while he witnesses His creations and perceives the existence of his own self? God the Exalted said: "And in yourselves; will you not see?" [al-Dhariyat: 21].

If you incline to the side of morals, you see man, through his degradation, reach the bottom of abasement: from flattery when he covets, and from stinginess when he is sated, and from impatience when he fears, and from anxiety. How many souls have been made offerings to the gods, and how many female infants buried alive, and how many wives thrown into the fire along with their dead husbands. Is there, after the likes of this, any further baseness in morals and feebleness of judgment?

Attributing the returning to God the Exalted is a figurative attribution, because He brings into being the high causes and the system of their interaction and opposition within the subsidiary causes, until they reach the immediate causes, in the manner of attributing the extending and withdrawal of the shade to Him, the Exalted, in His saying: "Have you not seen how your Lord extended the shadow?" [al-Furqan: 45] up to His saying: "Then We withdrew it to Us, a gradual withdrawal" [al-Furqan: 46], and in the manner of the attribution in the saying of people: "The emir built the city of such-and-such."

It is also permissible that "asfala safilin" be a locative (adverbial of place), that is: a place lower than what the lowest dwell in; so the annexing of "asfala" to "safilin" is the annexing of the place to what dwells in it. "Asfala" is in the accusative by "radadnahu" in the manner of an adverbial of place, or by removal of the preposition, that is: to the lowest of the low; and that is the abode of punishment, like His saying: "Indeed the hypocrites are in the lowest level of the Fire" [al-Nisa: 145]. So "radd" is used metaphorically for the meaning of placing him in a place that he deserves, and the attribution of "radd" to God the Exalted on this aspect is literal.

I reckon that His saying the Exalted, "Then We returned him to the lowest of the low," was the basis from which Malik, may God have mercy on him, derived what 'Iyad mentioned in al-Madarik. He said: Ibn Abi Uways said: Malik said: Rabi'ah approached me one day and said to me: "Who is the 'safilah' (base person), O Malik?" I said: "One who eats with his religion." He said to me: "Then who is the basest of the base?" I said: "One who makes others eat with his religion." So he said: "Zih" [an exclamation of approval], and he struck my chest (i.e., he struck my chest, meaning in approval). And that the polytheists were the lowest of the low because their great men and their leaders shaded them, so they made the worship of idols seem attractive to them, in order that they might attain their leadership.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 95, verse 6:**

﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds, for they will have a reward that is never cut off.﴾

This is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*, an exception whose excluded item belongs to the same category as what precedes it) from the generality (*'umum*) of "man." When He reported of man that he is returned to the lowest of the low, and then excepted from that generality those who believe, those who do not believe remain in the lowest of the low.

The meaning is that those who believed, after having been returned to the lowest of the low during the days of polytheism, returned through faith to the primordial nature (*fitra*) upon which God created man, and so they returned to their origin, the best of stature (*ahsan taqwim*).

The phrase "and did righteous deeds" is conjoined because the doing of righteous deeds is part of the best of stature after the coming of the Law (*shari'a*), since it strengthens the primordial nature in its firmness, and faith extends to moral conduct, returning it to its virtue and then guiding it to an increase in the best of virtues. In a hadith: "I was sent only to complete the noble characteristics of morality" (ﷺ).

So the conjunction of "and did righteous deeds" serves as praise of the believers, that their faith moves them to righteous action, and this was the condition of the believers at the time the surah was revealed. Thus this conjunction is a conjunction of a descriptive clause that reveals (*'atf sifa kashifa*).

There is no possibility here that the exception is disconnected, because the presence of the particle *fa* in His saying, ﴿so for them is a reward that is never cut off﴾, rejects that completely.

The report that they are not among those who are returned to the lowest of the low is made a consequence of the meaning of the exception, that a great reward is theirs, because the exception indicates that they are not among the lowest of the low, so further explanation is intended of their excellence and what has been prepared for them.

The tanwin on *ajr* (reward) is for magnification.

*Mamnun* means that which is bestowed upon the one rewarded with it as a favour, i.e., a reward that is not mixed with any turbidity, and there is no turbidity in being reproached with a statement such as "this is your reward" or "this is your gift." So *mamnun* is a passive participle from *manna 'alayhi* (he bestowed a favour upon him). It may also be a passive participle from *manna al-habl*, if he cut the rope, so it is *manin*, i.e., cut off or on the verge of being cut off.

*[Page 430]*

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 95, verses 7–8:

﴿So what can make you deny the Judgment after this?﴾ ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') drawn from everything mentioned about the creation of man in the finest form and then his being returned to the lowest of the low. What follows the fa' (the "so") is a statement caused by the explanation that precedes it. The meaning is: it has become clear to you that those who did not believe are the ones who were returned to the lowest of the low, so who among them would deny the true religion after this explanation?

The particle (ma) may be interrogative, and the interrogation is a rebuke. The address is to the human being mentioned in His saying: (﴿We created man in the finest form﴾ [al-Tin: 4]). After the believers were excepted from him, the denying human being remained.

The pronoun of address is an iltifat (a shift from third person to second person). The apparent form would be "so what makes him deny," but the purpose of the shift here is that it is more direct in confronting the denying human with rebuke.

The meaning of (yukadhdhibuka) is: makes you a denier, i.e., you have no excuse for denying the Judgment.

The object of the denial is either omitted because it is evident, meaning: makes you a denier of the Messenger (ﷺ), or it is the prepositional phrase with (bi), meaning: makes you a denier of the religion of Islam, or a denier of the recompense, if religion (din) is understood as recompense.

The sentence (﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾) is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) for threat and warning.

Din may mean creed or sacred law (shari'ah), as in His saying: (﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]) and His saying: (﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85]).

In that case the (ba') is causal, meaning: whoever denies you after this because of what you have brought of the religion, then God will judge concerning it.
